title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Oct 16, 2026
intro: Harness and context design, not model choice, is this week's lever for agent quality; trust and cost controls follow the same layered pattern.

cards.title: Add self-verification and tracing to your agent harness before swapping models
cards.problem: Coding-agent scores often stall because the harness, not the model, is the weak link.
cards.apply: Add a verification step that makes the agent check its work against the task spec before finishing, trace every run, and use the traces to trim context that distracts the agent.
cards.result: LangChain moved its coding agent from Top 30 to Top 5 on Terminal Bench with harness changes alone.

evidence.note: LangChain reports the Top 30 to Top 5 Terminal Bench move from its harness changes.

cards.title: Offload and summarize context instead of keeping every tool result in the window
cards.problem: Long-running agents degrade as tool outputs and history pile up in the context window.
cards.apply: Write large tool results to files and keep a pointer, summarize older turns at a threshold, and move specialized work into subagents so each context stays focused.
cards.result: The agent keeps working on the current step without drowning in stale output, and token use per turn drops.

evidence.note: Editorial inference from LangChain's context-engineering guidance; no figures claimed.

cards.title: Test behavior carryover before switching models mid-session
cards.problem: Swapping to a cheaper model mid-session passes along a history the new model may imitate, including the old model's habits.
cards.apply: Before routing sessions between models for cost, replay a sample of real multi-session histories through the swap and compare behavior, not just task success, against a fresh start on the recipient.
cards.result: You catch inherited quirks before a cost-driven model switch ships to users.

evidence.note: Editorial inference from the paper's framing that model swaps transfer history effects; no figures claimed.

cards.title: Layer agent autonomy: scope, bound, observe, then prove
cards.problem: Teams hold agents back because one failed action in production is costly and hard to explain afterward.
cards.apply: Grant each agent the narrowest tool and data scope, enforce hard limits outside the prompt (spend, rate, allowed actions), log every action for audit, and widen autonomy only as the audit trail earns it.
cards.result: Autonomy grows in steps you can justify, and any incident traces back to a specific boundary.

evidence.note: Editorial inference from AWS's Trust in Depth layers (scope, know, bound, observe, prove).

cards.title: Pair offline evals with online evals on production traces
cards.problem: Offline test sets miss the failure modes real users trigger, and judge runs get expensive fast.
cards.apply: Keep a small offline suite as a release gate, run cheap code-based evaluators on every production trace, and reserve LLM judges for a sampled subset and multi-turn conversations.
cards.result: Regressions surface from real traffic while judge spend stays bounded.

evidence.note: Editorial inference from LangChain's agent-evals Q&A; no figures claimed.

cards.title: Cap generative AI function spend before running LLM calls over whole tables
cards.problem: A single SQL query that calls an LLM per row can quietly run up a large bill.
cards.apply: Set per-query and per-project cost limits on BigQuery generative AI functions and test the query on a small sample to estimate spend before running it on the full table.
cards.result: Bulk classification jobs stop at a known ceiling instead of surprising you on the invoice.

evidence.note: Editorial inference from Google Cloud's announcement of cost management for generative AI functions.
